doc.title: Dick Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Jazz in New York today and gigging with a drumset
summary: Dixieland survives only at the Cajun and Arthur's Tavern; he lives in East Islip, hauls drums, is paid twenty-five dollars, and plays with Lee Lorenz.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: What’s the jazz scene like in New York City now?

Oh for my kind of music it’s pretty dim, dismal. There’s the Cajun at Eighth Avenue and Sixteenth Street where they always have some Dixieland band and I get hired as a substitute down there a lot. But outside of that, and Arthur’s Tavern, those are the only two places that have Dixieland now.
I live in Long Island in East Islip Long Island, it’s about fifty miles out from New York City.
So I’m fairly spoiled in this area you know, in fact one of the gigs I play as a pianist —
Oh I forgot you play piano.

Yeah. I actually work more as a piano player these days, and I play the Hotel Utica, and I literally can leave my house 15 minutes before the job, and unless I run into a stoplight I can sit down at the piano in time to start. But for you, with a drumset, to go into Manhattan—
No the drumset’s there. Oh, oh, these other jobs like the Cajun and Arthur’s, yes I bring it in there. That’s a struggle.
Yeah. Finding a parking spot and all that. You probably have to leave like—
Yeah and I get paid twenty-five dollars for it. You know.
Yeah. But I do it to help out and to play with these guys that I love.
These are my buddies from my band, they’re all in other bands. Lee Lorenz is one, he’s called me a few times, the great cartoonist. The next time you see the New Yorker, take a look for Lee Lorenz.
